text: Every linked service you've built this course needed some real form of credential — a connection string, a key, a password. Managed identities genuinely eliminate that: Data Factory gets its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, and other Azure services can grant that identity access directly — no credential to store, rotate, or ever leak.

Every data factory created through the portal automatically gets a system-assigned managed identity, tied directly to that factory's own lifecycle — delete the factory, and Azure deletes the identity with it. You'll find three real identifiers under Properties: an Object ID and Application ID identifying the identity itself, and a Tenant ID identifying which Microsoft Entra tenant it belongs to.

Having an identity does genuinely nothing by itself — it needs to actually be granted access, the same way you'd grant access to a person. On the target resource, open Access control, add a role assignment, select Managed identity as the member type, search for your data factory by name, and pick the narrowest role that actually does the job.

Once your factory's identity has Get and List permissions on a Key Vault's secrets, any linked service can reference a secret there instead of storing it directly. Toggle from Password to Azure Key Vault, pick the Key Vault linked service, and name the secret — Data Factory fetches the actual value at runtime.

Notice what's genuinely absent from this JSON: no actual password string anywhere. Only a secret name and a reference to the Key Vault linked service that actually holds it — the real value never touches the pipeline definition itself.

An automatic identity, a real role assignment, and secrets that live in Key Vault instead of in plain text. Next: RBAC — who can actually do what to your data factory itself, not just what your data factory can do to everything else.
